In this lesson, you will learn about the operation of a typical voltage regulator circuit that is adjustable.
INTRODUCTIONM
Regulator circuits provide a constant output voltage even when the input voltage or the output current varies.
Circuit operation is based on changing the effective resistance of the circuit when input and output conditions vary.
Let's begin the lesson on VOLTAGE REGULATOR OPERATION.....................
LESSON MENU
VOLTAGE REGULATOR CIRCUIT
This is a typical variable series voltage regulator circuit.
DISCUSSION
Q1 is the component that automatically changes resistance to maintain a constant Vout.
The output voltage of a rectifier filter is applied to the collector of Q1.
The load is connected to the emitter of Q1.
Current flow is from the rectifier filter to Q1, RL and then to ground.
Current flow is from ground, through RL and Q1, to the rectifier filter.
Since RL and Q1 are in series, this circuit is a series voltage regulator.
R1, Q2 and D1 form a voltage divider that applies base bias to Q1. Collector bias is obtained directly from the rectifier filter output voltage...
The emitter voltage for Q1 is developed by the action of the transistor.
R2 is used to vary the conduction of Q2 which changes Q2's collector to emitter voltage drop.
The operation of this variable series voltage regulator is based on two principles.
Let's investigate the operation of D1 and Q2 first.
The voltage applied to the base of Q1 is determined by the voltage drop of D1 and Q2.
D1's voltage drop is established by the Vz of the zener diode.
Recall that a zener diode maintains a constant voltage drop as long as it is operating in the breakdown region.
For example, if the zener voltage for D1 is 6V, the voltage between the cathode and ground of D1 is 6V.
The voltage drop across Q2 is established by the level of voltage applied to the base.
Recall that in a transistor, if the forward bias increases, collector current increases, decreasing the voltage on the collector.
Recall that in a transistor, if the forward bias increases, collector current increases, decreasing the voltage on the collector.

VOLTAGE ON COLLECTOR OF Q2 - Increasing the forward bias causes emitter to collector current to increase. When Ic increases, the voltage drop across R1 increases. This reduces the voltage on the collector which reduces Ece.
For example, the base voltage on Q2 establishes a collector to emitter voltage of 3 V.
The voltage drop of D1 and Q2 place 9 V on the base of Q1. The current flow set by D1 and Q2 causes R1 to drop 6 V.
If the input voltage increases to 18 V, D1 and Q2 currents change so that R1 drops 9 V, leaving 9 V on the base of Q1. Remember, Ee remains at 6V and Eb remains at 6.6 V.
If the input voltage decreases to 12 V, D1 and Q2 currents change so that R1 drops 3 V, leaving 9 V on the base of Q1.
In other words, the base voltage for Q1 is always 9 V as long as the DC input voltage is 9 V or greater.
Only when the voltage across Q2 is changed is the base voltage on Q1 changed.
Now, let's investigate the action of Q1.
With a base voltage of +9 V, the emitter is placed at +8.4 V.
If the input voltage is +18 V, the action of Q1 drops 9.6 V from the collector to emitter.
If the input voltage increases to 19 V, Q1 must drop 10.6 V. In effect, Q1 collector to emitter resistance is increased.
If the input voltage decreases to 17 V, Q1 must drop 8.6 V. In effect, Q1 collector to emitter resistance is decreased.
The result is that the output voltage, voltage on the emitter, is held constant even if the input voltage varies.
Also, if the load current varies, the output voltage is held constant by the action of Q1.
Again, the voltage on the emitter, which is the output voltage, is established by the action of Q1.
If the load current increased (due to RL decreasing), the emitter voltage would try to decrease because the load drops less voltage.......................
When Ee tries to decrease, the forward bias of the base-emitter PN junction increases, decreasing transistor resistance........................
With the transistor having less resistance, it drops less voltage.
Which means that RL drops more voltage, keeping the emitter at
If the load current decreased (due to RL increasing), the emitter voltage would try to increase because the load drops more voltage.ease because the load drops less voltage.
When Ee tries to increase, the forward bias of the base-emitter PN junction decreases, increasing transistor resistance......................
With the transistor having more resistance, it drops more voltage.
Which means that RL drops less voltage. Keeping the emitter at
The result is that the output voltage, on the emitter, is held constant even if the output current varies.
Putting the circuit together, D1 and Q2 set the voltage of the regulator. Notice the voltage across Q2 is variable.
Q1 maintains the output voltage to .6 V less than the voltage on its base under varying input and output conditions..
There is one additional point to bring out about the circuit. The voltage on the base of Q2 is always the same, .6 V above the emitter voltage! Let's see why.
The circuit is set up as shown. The output voltage is 8.4 V.
Increasing the resistance of R2 raises the voltage on the base of Q2.
With 7.6 V on the base, the base to emitter forward bias is increased, increasing emitter to collector current.
With 7.6 V on the base, the base to emitter forward bias is increased, increasing collector to emitter current.
An increase in collector current increases the voltage drop across R1, lowering Q2's collector voltage - Ece decreases.
The voltage on the base of Q1 is lowered to 8V.
The 8 V on the base of Q1 produces a 7.4 V output voltage. The regulated output voltage is lowered.
The lower output voltage lowers the voltage across R2, which lowers the base voltage of Q2 back to 6.6V.
The overall effect is that Eb is held to .6V above the emitter voltage (which is held to a constant level by D1) no matter what the value of R2 is.
Since R2 is changed and the voltage is held constant, the base current increases and decreases as R2 is increased and decreased.
Reversing the diode and the type of transistor does not change circuit operation.
The only difference is the circuit is now a negative voltage regulator.

VOLTAGE REGULATOR OPERATION
The purpose of this experiment is to demonstrate the normal operation of a variable voltage regulator.
EXPERIMENT
In this experiment, you will use two PC cards. One is a rectifier and the other is the variable voltage regulator.
Pick up the PC130-23 card and compare it to the schematic shown. This card is used as the rectifier and is placed in the PC1 position.
Pick up the PC130-26 card. This card is used to demonstrate variable voltage regulator circuits and is placed in the PC2 position.
Compare the card with the schematic shown.
Notice Q1 on the card and schematic. Q1 is a power transistor.
Since the transistor is in series to the load, total current flows through Q1.
Q1 is large so that more heat can be dissipated. Power transistors handle more current than regular transistors.
D1 and Q2 set the output voltage. Vz for the diode on the card is 4.7 V.
Notice that D1 and Q2 are small. Remember, they are in the base circuit of Q1 where current flow is usually in the micro amps.
Resistors R6, R7 and R8 along with switches S1 and S2 select the value of the load that is connected to the emitter of Q1.
R3, R4 and R5 form a voltage divider that applies the base voltage to Q2.
R2 feedbacks some of Vout to the cathode of D1. This ensures that D1 is always operating in the breakdown region or above Vz.
C1 and C2 ensure that any small voltage variations from R4 and D1 are not felt on the output; they act as a filter. Let's start the experiment.
